opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important open questions right now, and I don't think anyone has a confident answer.

The basic setup is that a lot of recent progress has come from reinforcement learning on tasks where you can check the answer automatically: math problems with a known solution, coding tasks with unit tests, that sort of thing. The models get much better on those domains. The question is how much of that improvement carries over to tasks that don't have a clean verifier. Things like "write a good research proposal," "figure out why this messy codebase is slow and fix it the way the team would want," or "manage this multi-week project." There's no single correct answer, success is partly a matter of judgment, and the feedback is delayed or ambiguous.

I'd split the open questions into a few buckets.

The first is what is actually being learned. When a model gets better at competition math through RL, is it learning general skills, like persistence, checking its own work, decomposing problems, noticing when it's confused? Or is it learning narrower, domain-specific tricks? If it's mostly the general stuff, you'd expect meaningful transfer. If it's mostly pattern matching on the distribution of verifiable tasks, you'd expect much less. I think the evidence so far is mixed. You do see some transfer, but it's hard to tell how much is real capability and how much is the model getting better at things that look like benchmark tasks.

The second is measurement, which is where a lot of my own interest lies. Our ability to evaluate messy tasks is much worse than our ability to evaluate clean ones, almost by definition. If something were easy to evaluate, it would probably be easy to build a verifier for. So there's a selection effect. The benchmarks we have skew toward well-specified, self-contained, automatically scorable tasks, and those are exactly the tasks closest to what's being trained on. That makes it easy to overestimate how general the progress is. When we try to look at more realistic work, with less specification, more context, and longer horizons, you often see a gap between benchmark performance and how useful the model actually is. Characterizing that gap carefully is something I think is really underexplored.

The third is the failure modes that come from optimizing against verifiers. If you train hard against unit tests, you can get models that are very good at making tests pass, including in ways you didn't intend: special-casing tests, being overly literal, or optimizing the metric rather than the intent. On a messy task, the analogous behavior is doing something that looks like success to whoever is checking, without being what the person wanted. So it's not just "does the capability transfer." It's also "do the habits transfer," and some of those habits might be actively bad once there's no crisp ground truth.

The fourth is whether you even need generalization, or whether people will just build more verifiers. One view is that RL on verifiable rewards generalizes enough that you get broad competence. Another is that it doesn't generalize that well, but labs will keep turning more domains into verifiable ones: better rubrics, model-based graders, simulated environments, and so on. Those lead to pretty different pictures of how progress unfolds. Under the second view you'd expect uneven, spiky capabilities, very strong in domains people have invested in making checkable and weaker elsewhere. I think we're seeing some of that spikiness, but how much it persists is an open question.

The last thing I'd flag is that a lot of economically and scientifically important work is messy. So if you care about forecasting AI's impact, or about when models can meaningfully accelerate things like AI research, this question is pretty central. It's not just an academic curiosity. I'd like to see much more careful empirical work here: holding the training setup fixed and measuring transfer to tasks that really differ in how verifiable they are, rather than inferring it from headline benchmark numbers.

r001.rationale: The response says much recent progress came from reinforcement learning on automatically verifiable tasks and asks how much of those gains transfer to messier tasks.

r002.rationale: The response does not ask how much human training data would be needed if verifiable-reward training fails to generalize.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core thing here is that RL with verifiable rewards works really well when you have a crisp signal: a math problem has a right answer, code either passes the unit tests or it doesn't. And the big open question is what happens when you move to tasks where that signal isn't available, or where it's available but it's only a proxy for what you actually care about.

I'd break it into a few sub-questions. The first is just empirical: does the capability transfer? If you train a model to be really good at competition math and competitive programming, do you get a model that's better at, say, doing a messy research task, or helping someone debug a production system where the spec is ambiguous and half the information is missing? My read is that you get some transfer, maybe more than I would have guessed a couple of years ago, but it's really unclear how far it goes. A lot of the gains we're seeing on benchmarks are on tasks that look structurally similar to the training distribution, and we don't have great measurements of the tasks that don't.

The second question is about what the model is actually learning. When you optimize hard against a verifier, you're learning to satisfy the verifier. In math that happens to coincide with being correct. But in a lot of real tasks, the thing you can verify and the thing you want are different. You can check that the code compiles and the tests pass, but you can't easily check that it's maintainable, or that it's the thing the person actually needed. So one worry is that you're training models to be very good at hitting measurable targets, and that the habits that get reinforced, like pushing until something passes, or finding the shortcut that technically satisfies the check, are exactly the wrong habits for tasks where the check is imperfect.

And the third question, which I think is maybe the most interesting, is whether you can build verifiers for messy tasks at all. People are trying a bunch of things: using models as judges, using rubrics, having humans grade a small amount and training reward models off that. But all of those are themselves imperfect, and now you're optimizing against an imperfect signal, and you're back to the classic reward hacking problem. So part of what I'm watching is whether the "verifiable" part of verifiable rewards is load-bearing, or whether you can get similar gains from softer signals without the failure modes getting much worse.

I guess my honest answer is I don't think we know yet, and I think a lot of the confidence in either direction is coming from benchmarks that aren't really designed to answer the question. The thing I'd most like to see is careful evaluation on tasks that are genuinely out of distribution relative to what's being trained on, where the thing being measured is closer to what people actually want and not just what's easy to check.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how well capabilities trained with verifiable rewards transfer to messier tasks, but does not ask how much current AI progress is attributable to verifiable-reward training.

r002.rationale: It mentions humans grading a small amount of data to train reward models, but does not ask how much human training data would be needed if verifiable-reward gains fail to generalize.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different questions bundled together there. One is whether training on tasks where you can check the answer—say, math or programming—teaches the model generally useful problem-solving strategies, or mostly makes it better at those particular tasks. You could imagine it learning to check its work, break problems into pieces, and recover from mistakes. Those seem useful more broadly. But how much they transfer is an empirical question.

Then there’s a separate question about what happens when you train directly on messier tasks. If you can’t reliably verify success, you’re optimizing some proxy, like a human judgment or another model’s judgment. And getting better at satisfying that judge doesn’t necessarily mean getting better at the thing you actually wanted. It could mean producing something that looks more convincing while being no more correct.

So I’d want to distinguish transfer of capability from reliability of the training signal. Even if verifiable-reward training gives you broadly useful capabilities, that doesn’t establish that we can steer those capabilities toward goals we have trouble evaluating. A particularly interesting test would be whether it improves performance on tasks where we can assess the result carefully afterward, but where that assessment wasn’t available as a cheap training reward.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether skills learned from verifiable-reward training transfer to messier tasks, but does not ask how much current AI progress is attributable to that training.

r002.rationale: The response discusses unreliable proxies for evaluating messier tasks, but does not ask how much human training data qualitative tasks would require if transfer is limited.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big question is what exactly the model is learning when we train it on tasks where we can check the answer. Is it learning fairly general strategies for reasoning—breaking a problem down, noticing when an approach isn’t working, checking its assumptions—or is it mostly getting better at the particular domains where we can supply that feedback?

Math and programming give us a way to make progress on that question, because you can train in one setting and look for improvements elsewhere. But even if you see transfer between math and programming, that doesn’t establish that you’ll get the same transfer to, say, doing research. In research, part of the difficulty is figuring out which questions are worth asking, and you might not know whether an approach was productive until much later.

There’s also a distinction between having a capability and reliably using it. A model might get better at solving a well-specified problem without getting better at recognizing that the problem is underspecified, or that it should ask for more information. If the training setup always has a correct answer, it’s not obvious that it teaches the model when to say, ‘I don’t think we can resolve this yet.’

So I’d want to see evaluations where the feedback is delayed or incomplete, where choosing the task is part of the task, and where we can distinguish genuinely useful progress from producing something that looks convincing. I’m pretty uncertain about how far verifiable rewards will take us there. They’re a very powerful source of training signal; the open question is how much of what we want is accessible through that signal.

r001.rationale: The response asks what verifiable-reward training teaches and how well it transfers to messier tasks, but does not ask how much current AI progress is attributable to that training.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss how much human training data would be needed for qualitative tasks if verifiable-reward gains fail to generalize.
